title: Jim Crow
objective: After this level you can explain how segregation laws, Plessy v. Ferguson and voting barriers undid Reconstruction's gains, and how Ida B. Wells fought back.
summary: Homer Plessy’s planned 1892 challenge led to Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which allowed segregation. Poll taxes and literacy tests shut out Black voters, and Ida B. Wells exposed lynching.

cards.headline: In 1892, a New Orleans man sat in the “wrong” train car on purpose.
cards.body: Homer Plessy was testing a law. His case would decide whether states could segregate Americans by race.

cards.headline: A planned challenge
cards.body: Louisiana’s Separate Car Act of 1890 required separate railway cars for Black and white passengers. A New Orleans civil rights group, the Comité des Citoyens, recruited Homer Plessy to test it. In 1892 he sat in a whites-only car. The arrest was the plan, not the problem.

cards.headline: “Separate but equal”
cards.body: In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 1 that segregation was constitutional if facilities were “equal.” The lone dissenter, Justice John Marshall Harlan, wrote: “Our Constitution is color-blind.” The majority’s rule became the legal backbone of Jim Crow.

mascot.line: Keep this: the 13th Amendment ended slavery, but Plessy let states write inequality into law.

cards.headline: Closing the ballot box
cards.body: From Mississippi in 1890 to Georgia in 1908, every former Confederate state moved to disfranchise Black voters. Their tools were poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses, which kept Black men from voting without saying “race” in the law.

cards.headline: Ida B. Wells fights back
cards.body: In 1892 a Memphis mob lynched Ida B. Wells’s friend Thomas Moss and two other Black grocers who competed with a white-owned store. Wells investigated lynchings and found the usual excuse for them was almost always false. A mob destroyed her newspaper’s office; she published anyway, in the pamphlet Southern Horrors. In 1909 she took part in founding the NAACP.

cards.headline: Jim Crow: explained
learned: Poll taxes and literacy tests blocked Black voters
Ida B. Wells exposed the lies behind lynching

questions.prompt: Match each person or group with their part in the fight over Jim Crow.

pairs.right: A New Orleans civil rights group

questions.explanation: Homer Plessy sat in a whites-only car, Justice Harlan wrote “Our Constitution is color-blind,” Ida B. Wells published Southern Horrors, and the Comité des Citoyens was the New Orleans civil rights group that recruited Plessy.

questions.prompt: How did Southern states keep Black men from voting after 1890?

options.label: By repealing the right to vote for all men in the South
With poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses
By ending elections for state offices altogether
options.rationale: The barriers were legal tests and fees.

options.label: By moving all Southern elections to Washington, D.C.

questions.explanation: Poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses kept Black men from voting.

questions.prompt: The 13th Amendment abolished slavery in 1865. What did the Plessy ruling allow 31 years later?

options.label: State laws segregating Black and white Americans
The return of slavery in the Southern states
An end to segregation on trains and in public schools
Voting rights for women across the country
options.rationale: The case was about segregation, not voting.

questions.explanation: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld state segregation laws as “separate but equal.”
